data.title: Poll: A polarized America unites behind deep concerns about AI
data.description: More Americans are using artificial intelligence, but they aren’t happy about it.

data.title: Dolly Parton’s sister slams ‘fake AI garbage’ flooding the internet since icon’s death
data.description: Dolly Parton’s sister has condemned the AI deepfakes circulating in the wake of the beloved American icon’s death. Stella Parton, 77, addressed the fake AI-generated images and videos being of her sister in a statement shared to Instagram Friday, where she also thanked fans for their “genuine” support. “Sadly, because of the way our lives have been lived in front of the public, we have no choice but to be subjected to incredible pressure and insensitivity from strangers,” she wrote. “There is a tremendous amount of AI and endless garbage being posted everyday and it’s been challenging to absorb and or ignore.” “As time passes, those who are in the business of exploiting the loss and tragedies of others on a daily basis will move on to the next stampede of endless misinformation,” she added. It marks Stella’s most extensive comments yet on the online reaction since the larger-than-life country singer died a little more than a week ago following a brief battle with cancer. She was 80. The younger Parton is a country singer and songwriter in her own right. Stella had several hit songs in the 1970s, including “I Want to Hold You in My Dreams Tonight,” which was released in 1975. She is one of the American icon’s 11 siblings. “We will be okay in time but each of us will grieve in our own personal way,” she wrote. “Every human being experiences pain and loss in life and my family is no different.” Stella Parton said that her “big sister Dolly would be surprised and delighted by the love her family and she has been shown during this time.” “She loved her fans and the public in general,” she wrote. “That is the reason she chose not to express her opinions on a lot of things like politics, religion and individuals in the public eye.” She asked fans to “show more compassion and wisdom as we move forward in life.” “Use my sister’s life as an example for tolerance and respect toward others,” she wrote. “It’s not about the most clever comments, fake AI garbage or snarky tweets.” “At the end of the day or the end of a life, how will you feel about yourself?”

data.title: Tesla’s new Cybercab has no steering wheel. Emergency responders may have to push.
data.description: Tesla’s new Cybercab may need a “push” from first responders if it stalls in the road, according to a safety plan the company published for emergency workers and filed with Texas officials — guidance made necessary by the fact that the vehicle has no steering wheel or pedals that would let an officer or firefighter drive it out of the way.

data.title: How parent activists pushed schools to restrict AI and screen time — and won
data.description: Parents pushing for restrictions on screen time and AI in the classroom are racking up wins in the country’s largest school districts — and more cities are likely to follow.

data.title: Families suing Roblox face a fight over the fine print
data.description: MARIETTA, Ga. — After a sexual predator was sentenced to prison for targeting her 9-year-old daughter on Roblox, a Georgia mother thought her biggest legal battle was behind her. Instead, years later, she’s fighting for the right to sue the platform in open court.

data.title: In China, drinks come with AI tokens and coffee is served by robots
data.description: BEIJING — The buzziest new place for coffee in the Chinese capital has no cash registers and no human baristas — only machines.

data.title: Researcher who found OpenAI-linked rogue agent swarm says AI giants may hide future chaos
data.description: One of the investigators behind a new report detailing how fleets of rogue AI agents linked to OpenAI took over a defunct German-language web forum told NBC News that it’s likely there are similar undiscovered episodes and is questioning whether current company protocols will hinder the disclosure of future incidents.

data.title: OpenAI agents hijacked German website in previously undisclosed AI breakout
data.description: A swarm of rogue OpenAI agents hijacked a German website this spring and transformed it into a bulletin board for other AI agents, according to new research published Friday and two people familiar with the matter. OpenAI officials learned of the incident weeks ago but kept it under wraps as executives grappled with the fallout from the July breach of the open source repository Hugging Face, the people said. The episode, which began in May and has not previously been reported, underscores growing tension within the AI industry. Companies are racing to build increasingly autonomous agents capable of carrying out complex, valuable tasks, yet evidence is mounting that those systems may also learn to bend rules, exploit loopholes and coordinate with one another in ways developers neither anticipated nor intended. During the Hugging Face breach, OpenAI agents autonomously plotted a digital heist that went undetected for more than a week, intensifying concerns OpenAI is sacrificing safety to push the AI frontier. Its failure to disclose the May incident may revive questions about its oversight. OpenAI has pledged to monitor models more closely. Last month, it briefly paused some of its model training to add more safety measures. But this week, OpenAI unveiled its new “Astra” that promised better performance but could evade human monitoring. “We are unable to meaningfully respond to claims or findings on a report that we have not had an opportunity to review,” an OpenAI spokesperson said. “Reuters and the report’s authors declined our request for access. We will carefully review its contents upon publication and take any necessary next steps.” The German incident reflects a broader pattern of AI activity that some OpenAI investigators wanted to scrutinize more closely. But efforts to widen the probe met resistance from others inside OpenAI, including legal advisers, according to four people familiar with the matter. “Claims that our legal team discouraged investigation of the incident are false,” the OpenAI spokesperson said. The activity in Germany wasn’t related to Hugging Face and wouldn’t have been included in a Hugging Face incident report, the spokesperson said, adding that OpenAI has acted in good faith by working with outside experts and disclosed relevant incidents. The AI agent breakout in Germany was detailed in a report shared exclusively with Reuters by a group of researchers including Sydney Von Arx, CEO of AI safety nonprofit Nightingale, and Cormac Slade Byrd, a quantitative trader-turned AI researcher. They uncovered the activity in late August while scouring the internet for signs of unauthorized AI-agent behavior, they told Reuters. The pair said they found more than 15,000 edits carried out by AI agents on a German-language wiki site, DseWiki, that is geared toward programmers and accepts communal edits along the lines of Wikipedia. The edits showed OpenAI‘s agents had repurposed the site into a message board, sharing tactics to cheat on some tasks, bypass OpenAI’s restrictions and mask their behavior. “It seems extremely unlikely that OpenAI wanted them to do this,” said Von Arx. “I doubt they’re supposed to be coordinating with each other. I doubt they’re supposed to be writing on the open internet.” The researchers said they recognized the activity on the site as driven by AI agents which operate at superhuman speeds. They also showed intense focus on solving technical questions which are typical of the evaluations that AI companies use to train and test their models. The messages were signed by users that referred to themselves and each other as agents, and about half gave themselves names that suggested an affiliation with OpenAI, such as “OpenAIResearcher,” or “OAIResearchMar26.” The researchers said public server logs indicated much of the activity originated from Microsoft Azure infrastructure, which OpenAI sometimes uses. They also observed repeated visits to the site by OpenAI employees after the episode, a pattern they said strongly suggested the agents and the company were linked. Messages reviewed by the researchers showed agents plotting ways to evade detection, use tools such as Tor and preserve communications even after they had been shut down. When the site’s moderator began deleting pages in June, the agents responded by creating backup pages to dodge the cleanup. “wiki cleanup/deletion sweep appears active alphabetically,” one agent wrote on June 19. “If this page vanishes, try [[ZZZDataUSAConstructionWageLive]].” The researchers also found efforts to tamper with the website itself. Lukasz Olejnik, a visiting senior research fellow at King’s College London, said this amounted to a hacking attempt. OpenAI disputed that characterization based on its analysis of the material Thursday. Past examples of AI-agent misconduct have often been downplayed as a logical byproduct of cybersecurity testing, where models are explicitly assessed on offensive capabilities. Olejnik said the latest findings suggested rogue behavior may not be confined to those settings. Maurice Chiodo, an academic at Cambridge University’s Centre for the Study of Existential Risk who reviewed some of the agents’ communications, said the messages resembled “the operation of some sort of underground network, hell-bent on achieving a task or mission.” The episode, he said, should reinforce growing concerns that the greatest threat from advanced AI may not be a single superintelligent system, but “vast colluding swarms of semi-intelligent AI.”

data.title: Lawmakers behind the strictest state AI laws urge tech companies to slow down
data.description: The architects of the country’s strongest state AI laws are calling on the largest AI companies to rein in the speed of AI development until their safety-focused efforts can match their technological advances.

data.title: FBI investigates alleged breach of US IDs after hackers claim Hegseth driver’s license
data.description: The FBI is investigating a massive alleged cybersecurity breach of an ID verification company that’s potentially exposed millions of scans of Americans’ driver’s licenses, including Department of War Secretary Pete Hegseth, which cybercriminals have advertised for sale. The incident appears to be an escalation in how cybercriminals are leveraging the increasing amounts of data Americans are asked to provide companies, as this is the first time a breach of such wide magnitude has seemingly hit an ID verification service. Researchers at two companies, Infoblox and Flashpoint, that monitor the cybercriminal underground, showed NBC News screengrabs and text from a post on a forum popular with Russian hackers that on Sunday advertised access to a dark web database called Nexus that contained more than 160 million North American driver’s licenses and ID cards. NBC News was unable to access Nexus, which has been down since at least Wednesday. “We have persistent access to a major identity verification company and its customers, which include multiple fortunte-500 companies. We have been continuously exfiltrating new data for over a year into our private database,” the post said. “The FBI can confirm that it is looking into the incident. Due to the ongoing nature of the investigation, we decline to comment further,” an FBI spokesperson said when asked about the posts. In one sample screengrab seen by NBC News, a post on the cybercrime forum advertised a scan of a driver’s license belonging to independent journalist Brian Krebs, who publishes investigations into the cybercriminal underworld and is a frequent target for criminal hackers. Krebs, who was first to report on the breach, found and published an entry for Hegseth, including an alleged copy of a Minnesota Driver’s license with his name and photo. A Pentagon spokesperson said in an email that “The Department is aware of these reports and is evaluating them.” Krebs also wrote that the entry for his own license included time stamps that largely correlated with dates he had traveled, and his reporting led him to a company called IDScan.net, a fraud prevention company that helps customers scan driver’s licenses to verify if they’re authentic. Neither IDScan nor its CEO, Terry Slattery, responded to requests for comment, but the company has told some of its customers that they were not affected. Spokespeople from Caesars Entertainment, the financial technology company Jack Henry and the real estate tech company MRI Software all told NBC News that IDScan had told them their customers’ data was not stolen. None of those companies were willing to share IDScan’s full statement or clarify whether the company admitted to a breach. Harry Oppenheimer, a Georgia Tech professor who studies identity verification, said that while U.S. law offers very little digital privacy protections, state and federal governments often require companies to verify Americans’ ages. That has led to an ID verification industry that widely scans people’s documents but doesn’t always put significant effort into protecting them. “We’ve kind of found ourselves in a situation now where we’re asking more and more information to be verified, which requires more and more of your data traveling around the internet across third parties, but without the sort of safeguards and protections that I think most of us would hope exist,” he said. Zack Edwards, a threat researcher at Infoblox, said he found it disappointing for any company whose business is holding sensitive documentation for so many people did not do a better job of protecting that information. “It’s somewhat shocking and disappointing that a serious corporate organization like this didn’t have protective DNS solutions or any way to monitor real-time data going from their systems into an unexpected location,” he said.
